intro: You're looking for a business financial adviser near you, someone who can help you make sense of the financial decisions that come with running a company. Whether you're thinking about how to take money out of the business, protect your shareholding, or plan for the day you exit, an adviser can talk you through the options. iComply introduces you to a suitable UK financial adviser who will quote you directly, with fees given as price on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a business financial adviser usually need
need_lead: Business owners often look for an adviser when a financial decision feels bigger than a quick chat with an accountant can cover.
needs: You want to understand the most tax-efficient way to take profit out of your company, whether through salary, dividends, pension contributions or a mix.
You're considering setting up or reviewing a company pension scheme and want to know how employer contributions could work for you and your staff.
You have other shareholders and want to put shareholder protection in place so the business can carry on if one of you dies or becomes seriously ill.
You're starting to think about succession or exit planning and want to prepare early rather than leave it until you're ready to sell.
You want to make sure your personal protection, such as life cover or income protection, is set up in a way that works alongside the business.
context_heading: What to understand when searching for a business financial adviser near you
context: Financial advice in the UK is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Before you engage an adviser, check that they or their firm are authorised, or are an appointed representative of an authorised firm, on the FCA register. If something goes wrong, you can complain to the firm and then to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme may protect you if an authorised firm fails.

Advisers must tell you whether their advice is independent, meaning they consider the whole market, or restricted to certain products or providers. They must also explain how they charge. Qualifications such as Chartered status from the Chartered Insurance Institute or the Personal Finance Society, or certifications like CFP, show advanced training, but you should still ask about their experience with businesses like yours.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe your business, including its size and structure, so we can introduce you to an adviser with relevant experience.
Explain what you're hoping to achieve, such as extracting profit more efficiently, setting up a pension, arranging shareholder protection or planning an exit.
Mention whether you have other shareholders or business partners, as this affects the advice you may need.
Let us know if you already have financial arrangements in place, such as a pension or protection policies, that you'd like reviewed.
Say whether you'd prefer to speak to someone locally or are happy to work with an adviser remotely.
Include any particular concerns you have, such as wanting to keep costs clear or needing advice that fits around your other professional advisers.
questions_heading: Questions to ask the financial adviser
questions: Are you authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, and can you provide your firm's reference number so I can check the register?
Will you be giving independent advice or restricted advice, and what does that mean for the products you recommend?
How do you charge for your services, and will you give me a clear quote in writing before any work begins?
What experience do you have with business owners in my situation, particularly around profit extraction and pensions?
How would you approach shareholder protection if I have business partners?
What should I be doing now to prepare for a future exit or succession, even if it's several years away?

faqs.q: Do I need a business financial adviser or can my accountant help?
faqs.a: Your accountant can help with tax and accounts, but financial advice on pensions, investments and protection is a separate regulated activity. A business financial adviser can work alongside your accountant to cover those areas.

faqs.q: What does 'price on application' mean for the adviser's fees?
faqs.a: It means the adviser will quote you directly based on your circumstances and the work involved. You should ask for a clear explanation of how they charge before you commit to anything.

faqs.q: Can a financial adviser help with shareholder protection?
faqs.a: Yes, business financial advisers can arrange shareholder protection, which is a type of insurance designed to help buy out a shareholder's interest if they die or become seriously ill. It can help keep the business running smoothly.

faqs.q: How do I check that an adviser is properly regulated?
faqs.a: You can check the Financial Conduct Authority's register to see if an adviser or firm is authorised or is an appointed representative. The adviser should also tell you whether their advice is independent or restricted and how they charge.

extra_heading: Choosing a business financial adviser close to you
extra: Searching for a business financial adviser near you suggests you'd rather sit down face to face with someone who understands the local business landscape, or at least know that help is within reach. That's a reasonable instinct, but it's worth asking whether proximity matters more than relevant experience with businesses like yours. Many business owners find that the right adviser for their circumstances is worth travelling to, or working with remotely.

When you compare the advisers you're considering, look at what they actually do for business owners rather than just how close they are. Ask whether they regularly advise on profit extraction, company pensions, shareholder protection and exit planning, and whether they work alongside accountants and solicitors. Check each firm on the Financial Conduct Authority register, and ask directly whether their advice is independent or restricted and how they charge, so you can weigh up the options on your own terms.

A first meeting with a business financial adviser is usually a conversation rather than a sales pitch. Expect them to ask about your company's structure, your other shareholders, any existing pensions or protection policies, and what you want to achieve and by when. You shouldn't feel pressured to commit to anything at that stage, and it's fine to say you're speaking to more than one adviser before deciding.

extra_faqs.q: Does my business financial adviser need to be local to me?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. Working with someone nearby can make meetings easier, but what matters most is that they understand businesses like yours and can advise on the areas you need. Ask about how they'd work with you, whether in person or remotely, before you decide.

extra_faqs.q: Can a business financial adviser help if my company is small?
extra_faqs.a: Yes. Many of the issues business owners face, such as taking profit efficiently, setting up a pension or protecting a shareholding, apply whether the company has a handful of employees or many more. Describe your situation when you enquire so you're introduced to an adviser with relevant experience.
